keyVerseText: And in that same hour he cured many of their infirmities and plagues, and of evil spirits; and unto many that were blind he gave sight.
rootMeaning: The Greek verb χαρίζομαι (charízomai) derives from the noun χάρις (cháris), which means grace, favor, or kindness. As a middle voice verb, it conveys the idea of granting or giving freely and graciously, emphasizing an act done out of kindness or favor rather than obligation. This root sense enriches the common English glosses like "forgive" or "give" by highlighting the voluntary, gracious nature of the action — it is not merely a transaction but a gracious bestowal reflecting inner generosity.
usageInScripture: Across its 23 occurrences, χαρίζομαι consistently conveys acts of gracious giving, forgiving, or delivering. The top English translations include "I forgave," "forgiving," and "forgave," showing a strong emphasis on forgiveness, but also include "he gave" and "deliver," indicating a broader sense of granting or bestowing benefits. This range reveals the word’s flexibility to describe both tangible and intangible gifts, especially the gracious pardon of sins or the granting of favors, always highlighting the kindness and freedom inherent in the act.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding χαρίζομαι enriches our grasp of divine grace in the Christian faith. It underscores that God’s forgiveness and blessings are not earned but freely granted out of His gracious will, reflecting the very essence of grace (χάρις). This verb reminds believers that forgiveness is an act of kindness that rescues and restores, mirroring Christ’s redemptive work. The concept of granting favor or pardon graciously calls Christians to embody that same generous spirit in relationships, reflecting God’s character and mercy in the life of the church.
keyVerseReflection: In Luke 7:21, where Jesus heals many and gives sight to the blind, the use of χαρίζομαι highlights the gracious, free nature of His miracles and blessings. This word emphasizes that Jesus does not merely perform acts of power but graciously grants healing and restoration as a favor to those in need. It reveals the heart of Christ’s ministry — one marked by kindness and mercy, freely bestowing deliverance and blessing to the afflicted.
